name: Apple
summary: A deciduous fruit tree with many named cultivars. Cultivar, rootstock, pollination needs and chilling requirements vary; this species-level profile does not assign any one variety.

identity.guidance: Kew POWO accepts Malus domestica. NC State describes the common apple and notes that hundreds of cultivars differ in fruit traits and chilling requirements. This entry represents the species, not Honeycrisp, Gala, or another cultivar.

growth.short: Deciduous tree; final size depends strongly on rootstock
growth.guidance: NC State reports that seed-grown trees can reach 20 feet or more, while purchased trees are commonly grafted onto rootstocks that alter mature size. No single height is assigned to this rootstock-unspecified species record.

cultivation.short: Choose a locally suitable cultivar and rootstock; plan for pollination
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends selecting for local chilling requirements, full sun and a nearby compatible pollinizer for many cultivars. The profile does not claim a particular cultivar's chill hours or pollination compatibility.

propagation.short: Seedlings do not preserve a named apple cultivar
propagation.guidance: NC State describes purchased apple trees as grafted scion/rootstock combinations and lists both grafting and seed propagation. Grafting is the relevant route when preserving a named cultivar; no seed-starting protocol is represented here.

harvestUse.short: Edible fruit; harvest timing depends on cultivar
harvestUse.guidance: NC State describes apples for fresh and cooked use and lists cultivar-dependent seasons. This species-level page does not establish a universal harvest date.

care.short: Prune the canopy and thin heavy fruit set
care.guidance: UMN Extension recommends annual pruning to maintain tree health and structure and notes that thinning can improve fruit quality and reduce alternate bearing. Its calendar dates are Minnesota-specific, so use local timing rather than treating March or a particular thinning week as universal.

problems.short: Pollination, chill, pests and disease are site- and cultivar-dependent
problems.guidance: NC State notes disease and pest pressure and emphasizes that chilling requirements differ among cultivars. Use local extension recommendations for diagnosis and management rather than applying a cultivar-specific spray program to this generic record.

name: European Pear
summary: A deciduous fruit tree with many cultivars. The species profile distinguishes European pear from Asian pear and does not imply a particular cultivar, rootstock, or pollinizer pairing.

identity.guidance: Kew POWO accepts Pyrus communis. NC State uses common pear and European pear for this species; Asian pear is treated separately as Pyrus pyrifolia.

growth.short: Woody deciduous fruit tree; size depends on rootstock
growth.guidance: NC State reports about 40–50 ft tall and 25–35 ft wide for common pear; dwarfing rootstocks are commonly used, so a purchased tree may be smaller. These are species-level outdoor landscape dimensions, not a rootstock-specific guarantee.

cultivation.short: Full sun, well-drained soil and pollination planning
cultivation.guidance: NC State describes full-sun cultivation, broad soil tolerance with good drainage, and improved production from compatible pollinizers. Specific cultivar compatibility and regional disease pressure require local selection.

propagation.short: Grafting is the documented nursery route
propagation.guidance: NC State states that common pears are usually grafted to rootstocks and lists grafting as propagation. No seed-starting or seedling-establishment protocol is provided for this profile.

harvestUse.short: Edible fruit; harvest season varies by cultivar
harvestUse.guidance: European pears are harvested mature before they soften on the tree. USU describes a lighter-green skin cue and a gentle lift-and-twist check; fruit that separates easily is mature. Exact timing and later storage needs vary by cultivar, and Asian pears follow a different on-tree ripening pattern.

problems.short: Fire blight and other pests/diseases are relevant risks
problems.guidance: NC State lists fire blight and other disease and insect concerns. This is a species-level risk list, not a resistance claim for any cultivar.

care.short: Train young trees and thin fruit set
care.guidance: USU Extension describes central-leader training for home pears and hand-thinning early fruit: retain the largest fruit in a cluster and space fruit along branches. Its 2–3-week-after-petal-fall cue is Utah guidance; use local timing rather than treating that calendar as universal.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Orchard-tree guidance does not establish hydroponic suitability.

evidence.note: NC State describes common pear as a deciduous tree with an erect, spreading habit.

name: Asian Pear
summary: A distinct pear-tree species producing crisp fruit. Cultivars differ in texture, pollination and climate fit; this species profile does not identify a named Asian-pear cultivar.

identity.guidance: Kew POWO accepts Pyrus pyrifolia. NC State lists Asian pear, apple pear and Chinese pear as common names. It is distinct from European pear (Pyrus communis).

growth.short: Woody fruit tree; grafted rootstock affects mature size
growth.guidance: NC State notes that trees can exceed 20 feet depending on grafted rootstock and may live for decades. No one height or spread is assigned without a specified rootstock and cultivar.

cultivation.short: Full sun, fertile well-drained soil and frost-aware siting
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, with a site that limits late-spring frost exposure. Some cultivars self-pollinate but often crop better with another variety; cultivar compatibility is not established here.

propagation.short: Grafting is documented; no seed protocol is supplied
propagation.guidance: NC State lists grafting as the propagation strategy for Asian pear. Its profile does not provide a seed sowing or seedling-establishment protocol, so none is inferred.

harvestUse.short: Crisp edible fruit; maturity depends on cultivar
harvestUse.guidance: NC State describes Asian pear fruit as edible and notes that fruit can drop when ripe in windy or rainy weather. It does not establish a single cultivar-independent harvest date.

care.short: Train young trees to a balanced central leader
care.guidance: USU Extension recommends beginning training at planting and developing a central leader with well-spaced scaffold branches for home-orchard light distribution. This is orchard-tree training, not a container-pruning prescription; rootstock and local practice still matter.

problems.short: Fire blight and fruit drop may need attention
problems.guidance: NC State identifies fire blight as a principal disease concern and notes ripe-fruit drop in wind or rain. These are species-level cautions, not a cultivar resistance statement.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Orchard-tree guidance does not establish hydroponic suitability.

name: Peach
summary: Deciduous fruit tree with a broad range of peach and nectarine types. Cultivar and rootstock determine chilling, size, timing, and disease context; this species profile does not promise dwarf habit or a fixed harvest date.

identity.guidance: Kew POWO accepts Prunus persica. NC State notes that peaches and nectarines are forms within this cultivated species and lists many distinct cultivars; this record does not identify one.

growth.short: Fast-growing deciduous tree; cultivar and pruning affect form
growth.guidance: NC State reports a rounded tree commonly 15–25 feet tall and wide, with upward-growing branches. This is a regional species range, not a dwarf-container guarantee.

cultivation.short: Full sun, drainage and cultivar-appropriate chilling
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends full sun and moist, fertile, well-drained acidic soil and notes that cultivars require different chilling exposure. Select a locally appropriate cultivar; the generic profile cannot determine that requirement.

propagation.short: Cultivars are maintained on budded or grafted trees
propagation.guidance: NC State's orchard guide explains that the chosen cultivar (scion) is propagated onto a separate rootstock and recommends obtaining budded or grafted trees from a reputable nursery. A seed-grown peach is not evidence of the parent cultivar. Seed-starting belongs in the Seed Profile; rootstock and cultivar selection are nursery/orchard decisions.

harvestUse.short: Edible summer fruit; peach and nectarine forms differ by skin texture
harvestUse.guidance: NC State describes summer fruit and explains that a recessive trait produces smooth-skinned nectarines. This species record does not specify a named fruit type or harvest window for an individual cultivar.

problems.short: Late frost, pests and diseases can affect flowers and fruit
problems.guidance: NC State notes late-spring frost damage and lists insect and disease risks. Management depends on location and cultivar; no resistance trait is claimed.

management.short: Train an open center and manage fruit load
management.guidance: NC State describes open-center/vase training for peaches and recommends dormant-season structural pruning. It also explains that thinning fruit reduces undersized, lower-quality crops; the useful timing depends on bloom and local conditions. Remove diseased fallen fruit and wood during orchard sanitation. These are North Carolina orchard principles, not a cultivar-specific spray schedule.

harvest.short: Harvest by cultivar-specific maturity cues, not a universal date
harvest.guidance: NC State states that peach harvest timing and color/firmness cues vary by cultivar and season. Harvest selectively when fruit has reached the maturity needed for immediate use; the regional guide gives June–October as a broad North Carolina window, not a promise for this unspecified peach. Handle gently to avoid bruising.

name: European Plum
summary: A deciduous cultivated plum species, distinct from Japanese plum. Fruit color and use vary among cultivars; this species-level profile does not assign a greengage, damson, or prune cultivar.

identity.guidance: Kew POWO accepts Prunus domestica. NC State identifies common, European and prune plum as names for this species and notes that damson and greengage types are related infraspecific groups.

growth.short: Small deciduous tree or large shrub
growth.guidance: NC State reports a typical 10–20 ft height and width for European plum. Cultivar, rootstock and management affect the final size; this is broad outdoor landscape context, not a container or indoor-system dimension.

cultivation.short: Full sun and fertile, moist, well-drained soil
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends full sun and fertile, moist, well-drained soil. It notes later flowering relative to other plums, but local frost exposure and cultivar still matter.

propagation.short: Grafting, root cuttings and seed are listed; no seed protocol is given
propagation.guidance: NC State lists grafting, root cuttings and seed as propagation strategies. It does not specify a home seed-starting protocol; grafting is the documented route for maintaining a selected cultivar.

harvestUse.guidance: NC State describes plums for fresh or cooked use and for drying. Color and season depend on cultivar, so this profile does not set a universal harvest date.

problems.short: Plum pests and fruit/foliar diseases are reported
problems.guidance: NC State lists brown rot, rust, powdery mildew, codling moth and other potential problems. These are reported risks, not a claim of susceptibility for a particular cultivar.

care.short: Train an open canopy and thin an overloaded crop
care.guidance: Penn State Extension presents open-center training for home plums; better light and airflow can reduce conditions favorable to brown rot but do not guarantee disease control. Its regional thinning guide suggests removing excess fruit early, around 1/2 inch, and leaving roughly 6–10 inches between fruit; local cultivar and climate guidance takes precedence.

name: Japanese Plum
summary: A distinct plum-tree species whose cultivars often flower and ripen earlier than European plums. No named cultivar or pollination partner is specified.

identity.guidance: Kew POWO accepts Prunus salicina. NC State uses Japanese plum and Chinese plum and distinguishes it from European plum (P. domestica).

growth.short: Deciduous fruit tree with cultivar-dependent dimensions
growth.guidance: NC State reports regional dimensions around 20–33 ft tall and 15–30 ft wide; cultivar and location vary. The range is outdoor landscape context, not a named-cultivar or indoor-system footprint.

cultivation.short: Full sun and moist, well-drained soil
cultivation.guidance: NC State describes full-sun cultivation, moist well-drained soil, and earlier bloom/ripening than European plums. Frost exposure and cultivar suitability remain location-dependent.

propagation.short: Seed and stem cutting are listed; no germination protocol is supplied
propagation.guidance: NC State lists seed and stem cutting as propagation methods but does not provide a home seed establishment protocol. A seedling is not identified as a named fruit cultivar.

harvestUse.short: Edible fruit, generally ripening earlier than European plum
harvestUse.guidance: NC State describes edible fruit harvested in summer and notes that Japanese plum cultivars tend to ripen earlier than European plum cultivars. Exact timing remains cultivar-specific.

problems.short: Earlier bloom makes local spring-frost context worth checking
problems.guidance: NC State reports that Japanese plums flower earlier in spring than European plums. Garden adaptation: in frost-prone locations, compare local frost timing with the selected cultivar's bloom; this source does not establish a frost threshold, pollination partner, or cultivar resistance.

care.short: Use plum-specific training; check early bloom against local frost risk
care.guidance: Penn State presents open-center training as a home-plum option and explains its light/airflow purpose; this is broad plum guidance, not a named-cultivar trial. NC State reports Japanese plums bloom earlier than European plums, so checking local spring-frost exposure is a Garden adaptation, not a source-stated frost threshold.

name: Sweet Cherry
summary: A deciduous fruit tree grown for sweet cherries and spring flowers. Cultivar, rootstock and pollination requirements vary; this record is not a specific named cherry variety.

identity.guidance: Kew POWO accepts Prunus avium. NC State describes sweet cherry as an edible-fruit tree; cultivar-level characteristics are not applied to this species-level profile.

growth.short: Deciduous tree with spring flowers and summer fruit
growth.guidance: NC State reports about 15–30 ft in height with a matching spread for sweet cherry. Rootstock and cultivar are unspecified, so treat this as a broad outdoor landscape range rather than a prediction for a particular purchased tree.

cultivation.short: Full sun and moisture-retentive but well-drained soil
cultivation.guidance: NC State describes full sun and soil that retains moisture while draining well. Late frost can damage buds, and cultivar selection must account for local climate and pollination.

harvestUse.short: Edible sweet fruit; remove pits before processing
harvestUse.guidance: NC State describes sweet cherries as edible raw or cooked and warns that pits contain cyanogenic compounds. Remove pits before blending or processing in a way that could crack them.

problems.short: Late frost, pests and diseases can affect the crop
problems.guidance: NC State lists late-frost damage, birds/squirrels, insects and diseases. This broad risk list is not a cultivar-specific resistance or treatment prescription.

care.short: Prune after fruiting rather than copying other stone-fruit timing
care.guidance: Penn State Extension distinguishes sweet cherry from other stone fruits and recommends pruning after fruiting or around early July in its regional guidance. Treat the date as Pennsylvania-specific and follow local disease/climate advice; this does not establish a cultivar-specific training system.

pollination.short: Check cultivar compatibility; many sweet cherries need a pollinizer
pollination.guidance: Penn State Extension reports that most sweet-cherry cultivars are not self-fruitful and need a different, specifically compatible sweet-cherry cultivar whose bloom overlaps; some cultivars are self-fruitful, and a compatible second cultivar may still improve harvest. Sour cherries are not a reliable substitute because bloom periods usually do not overlap. Since this profile names no cultivar, it does not assign a pollinizer, compatibility group, or guarantee of fruit set. Protect pollinating insects during bloom.

name: Sour Cherry
summary: A deciduous, relatively cold-hardy cherry tree grown for tart fruit. Cultivar and regional conditions still affect size, harvest and disease pressure.

identity.guidance: Kew POWO accepts Prunus cerasus. NC State uses sour cherry and tart cherry and distinguishes it from sweet cherry (P. avium).

growth.short: Deciduous tree with a rounded crown
growth.guidance: NC State describes a rounded tree that may reach about 30 feet under its regional conditions. This is not a dwarf-rootstock or container dimension.

cultivation.short: Full sun and fertile, well-drained soil
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends full sun and fertile, well-drained soil and notes that sour cherry is more cold hardy than sweet cherry and is self-pollinating. This species-level statement does not identify a cultivar.

propagation.short: Seed is listed but no home sowing protocol is provided
propagation.guidance: NC State lists seed and grafting among propagation strategies but does not provide a seed-starting protocol. Grafting is the documented nursery route when a named cultivar is wanted.

harvestUse.short: Tart edible fruit, often used in cooking
harvestUse.guidance: NC State describes sour cherries as edible fresh or dried and commonly used in pies. Remove pits before processing; the source notes cyanogenic compounds in pits and other plant parts.

problems.short: Pest and disease pressure; protect ripening fruit
problems.guidance: NC State lists potential insects and diseases and notes bird feeding on mature fruit. These are reported risks, not a diagnosis or cultivar-level resistance claim.

care.short: Maintain an open canopy; do not thin tart cherries
care.guidance: Penn State describes open-center training as a suitable option for tart cherry and says improved light and airflow can help reduce brown-rot conditions. Its home-orchard thinning guidance explicitly says tart cherries should not be thinned; keep pruning and protection decisions local rather than applying a plum or sweet-cherry calendar.

name: Apricot
summary: A deciduous apricot tree with early spring bloom and edible stone fruit. USU Extension says most cultivars are self-fruitful, though a nearby cultivar blooming at the same time may improve yield. Early bloom remains frost-sensitive; this species-level record does not select a cultivar or promise fruit set.

identity.guidance: Kew POWO accepts Prunus armeniaca. NC State identifies apricot as a cultivated fruit-tree species and describes cultivar differences without assigning one to this record.

growth.short: Deciduous tree with a broad canopy
growth.guidance: NC State describes apricot trees as roughly 15–40 feet tall and wide in its regional account. Rootstock and cultivar can change dimensions; no container size is inferred.

cultivation.short: Full sun, well-drained soil and a frost-aware site; check cultivar pollination needs
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends full sun and moist, well-drained soil. Apricots bloom early and are vulnerable to spring frost; cultivar chill requirements and local conditions affect success. USU Extension says most apricot cultivars are self-fruitful, but a nearby cultivar with overlapping bloom may improve yield. Because this record does not identify a cultivar, confirm the requirements of the actual tree rather than assuming every apricot is self-fruitful.

propagation.short: Cuttings or grafting are documented alternatives
propagation.guidance: NC State states that apricot may be propagated by cuttings or grafting. Its page does not provide seed sowing instructions, so seed-starting fields remain unestablished.

harvestUse.short: Edible fruit ripens in early summer in the regional account
harvestUse.guidance: NC State describes edible apricots ripening from late June to July in its regional context. Timing varies by location and cultivar and is not a universal calendar.

care.short: Prune in late winter, retain productive spurs and thin an over-set crop
care.guidance: USU Extension describes annual late-winter pruning and open-vase training for apricots. Fruiting spurs can remain productive for several years, so avoid indiscriminate removal of fruiting wood. Apricots may over-set: when fruit is grape-sized (about 4–6 weeks after full bloom in USU's guidance), thin to roughly one fruit every 4–6 inches along each branch. This can improve the size of remaining fruit and reduce stress on the tree; timing is regional guidance, not a fixed calendar for every climate.

problems.short: Early bloom risks frost loss; wet roots can signal poor drainage or overwatering
problems.guidance: NC State emphasizes frost damage to early flowers and fruit buds. USU reports root-rot risk in wet, heavy soils or under overwatering; its Utah guidance also notes iron chlorosis in alkaline soils. These are context-dependent risks, not diagnoses: check recent weather, drainage, watering and local soil conditions before attributing decline, and no cultivar resistance is claimed.

name: Smooth Blackberry
summary: An eastern North American blackberry species with nearly smooth canes and edible fruit. It spreads by rhizomes and is distinct from raspberry and other plants sold under the broad name blackberry.

identity.guidance: Kew POWO accepts Rubus canadensis. NC State uses smooth blackberry and thornless blackberry and distinguishes it from the many other Rubus species also called blackberry. The species, not a named cultivar, is represented.

growth.short: Perennial subshrub with erect-to-arching canes and rhizomes
growth.guidance: NC State describes nearly smooth canes, compound leaves and rhizomes that can form thickets. This habit is species-level and does not imply a compact container form.

cultivation.short: Full sun and well-drained soil; allow room for spreading
cultivation.guidance: NC State's genus-level guidance says many Rubus prefer acidic, well-drained soil and full sun, while the species page notes rhizomatous spread. The soil guidance is genus-level, not a species-specific substrate prescription.

propagation.short: Rhizome spread is documented; no seed protocol is supplied
propagation.guidance: NC State describes underground rhizomes that spread and form thickets. The selected pages do not provide seed establishment instructions for this species; do not infer them from other blackberries.

maintenance.short: Shorten dead stems to support stem-nesting bees; leave them standing
maintenance.guidance: NC State reports that native bees nest in the dead, hollow stems of Rubus canadensis. It encourages cutting dead stems back to 12–24 inches (about 30–61 cm) and leaving them standing until they disintegrate naturally. This species-specific wildlife practice does not justify cutting living canes or applying a commercial blackberry pruning schedule to this wild species.

harvestUse.short: Edible berries can be eaten fresh or cooked
harvestUse.guidance: NC State describes the fruit as sweet and suitable raw or cooked. Do not generalize flavor to all blackberry species.

harvest.short: Pick fully ripe fruit; repeat checks as berries ripen
harvest.guidance: For cultivated blackberries, OSU Extension says fully ripe berries are generally dull black and separate with a gentle breaking motion. It recommends rechecking about every 4–7 days depending on cultivar and weather, more often in warm or rainy conditions, and refrigerating dry fruit promptly. This is crop-group guidance, not a ripeness guarantee or fixed schedule for wild Rubus canadensis.

problems.short: Rhizomes can form thickets; monitor local spread
problems.guidance: NC State notes rhizomatous spread. Its page does not determine invasiveness in every region; check local guidance before planting near natural areas.
